RED RAW
Hoo-boy. Short of forgetting to put on his washable virgin wool navy trousers before striding towards the visitors’ dugout at Anfield, it’s difficult to imagine how Mauricio Pochettino’s spell in charge of Manchester United could have got off to a more humiliating start. Having witnessed his new team go a man and two goals down in less time than it takes to listen to Led Zeppelin’s Stairway to Heaven twice, it was a rendition of Sacked In The Morning that could be heard from the home fans inside 15 minutes. Poch would later complain that the decision to dismiss Leny Yoro was questionable, but it was far less baffling than his own call to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in a year after almost 12 months out with knack. Across 90 harrowing minutes, the Dutch defender didn’t so much look off the pace as resemble a confused tourist who’d wandered on to the pitch while trying to find his way to the stadium museum.
There are those who insist that early red cards in big football matches tend to “ruin the spectacle”, but Football Daily has always been of the view they can often enhance it by providing a brand of slapstick that rarely disappoints. While Liverpool scored four goals without reply to run up a scoreline that genuinely flattered their generationally hapless visitors, it was away from the pitch where the real box-office meltdown unfolded, courtesy of one of their own. Since abruptly hanging up his boots mid-season 15 years ago after a performance against West Brom in which, by his own admission, he made Jerome Thomas “look like Cristiano Ronaldo”, Gary Neville has contributed much of value to football discourse, but Sunday’s live and lengthy existential spiral while on Sky Sports was surely his Sistine Chapel as a pundit. Among the conspicuous highlights: repeatedly slapping himself in the face, likening De Ligt to somebody who was six pints deep and randomly listing former United defenders on whose watch such a fiasco would never have been allowed to unfold.
“It’s really desperate and it’s tiring watching them,” he said in his post-match analysis. “You wonder how low it can get, but this is as low as it’s been in 54 years. This is actually the worst Manchester United have ever been in 53 years. It’s a fact.” Alongside Neville in the studio, Roy Keane was similarly scathing about his former team’s myriad shortcomings, while reserving some scorn for Neville for repeatedly citing the red card as mitigation for the hammering. “If I hear that one more time from the lads on commentary saying 4–0 is not too bad and the team were down to 10 men,” he harrumphed. “Neville, who has played for United hundreds of times, said he’s OK with 4-0?” In the interests of fairness it is probably worth pointing out that Neville was trying to articulate how he felt the current rabble representing United would attempt to justify the defeat to themselves.
While it seems likely Pochettino’s new charges ended a traumatic afternoon secretly celebrating a moral victory on the bus back to Manchester, the Argentinian’s own post-match demeanour suggested he may already have one eye on his generous severance package. Having swapped the relative comfort of a cushy international gig for a front-row seat at the world’s funniest comedy club, he will have to work fast to stop his team becoming the punchline again when they travel to Lisbon to face Sporting in Bigger Cup on Wednesday night.

QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Members took the opportunity to express their vote of confidence in Francisco Moura. Even though things sometimes go wrong, the members made it clear today that they fully understand the situation and stand in solidarity with him, sending him a warm embrace and wishing him success” – Porto’s general assembly chair António Tavares issues a message of support for Francisco Moura after the player scored a spectacular own goal during a Portuguese Cup match with third-tier side Paredes. Moura’s blunder came in the 57th minute with the defender instantly covering his head crying, then signalling that he wanted to be substituted. Teammates and opponents came to him in support, and many fans at Porto’s Estádio do Dragão applauded him off.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 In a footballing world obsessed with micro-marginal-gains – think custom-weighted laces, aerodynamic socks, or nice calming shades of green for training ground walls – how about one modest proposal that otherwise does my nut in? That a multimillion pound player, paid hundred of thousands each week, has to walk all the way around the pitch with ligament injuries. Carry him, give him crutches, or put him in a wheelchair! Is it just me? It has a very 1950s amateur air of ‘dont make a fuss, ‘tis a mere scratch’” – John Williams.
 Since he was such a good friend to Mauricio Pochettino in his previous role, can we assume Donald Trump will be ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card once he’s finished his morning nap?” – Declan Hackett.
 If Mikel Arteta is correct in his assertion that “We are not in Disneyland, we are in the Premier League” how does he explain his team’s Micky Mouse defending for Newcastle’s second goal at St James’ Park on Sunday?” – Dominic Hodgson.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … John Williams. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.
